title: I built OrgX on the wrong primitive
hook: i built my agent system on the wrong primitive. for months.
hypothesis: a confession/mistake hook plus a 'wrong primitive' reframe earns more founder trust + saves than a feature-list hook does for cold reach
caption:
the moment it clicked was watching a second agent pick up work a first one 'finished.' it had the files. it had the last message. and it still had no idea why any of it existed — what we'd already ruled out, what done even meant, who was allowed to approve the thing. and so i'm like, wait, i've been treating the prompt as the unit this whole time, but the prompt ends and the company doesn't. the goal + the decisions + the quality bar have to live somewhere that isn't a chat window that evaporates the second the context runs out. so orgx became the layer underneath claude / cursor / codex instead of another place to go type — a context pack instead of a transcript dump. i changed my mind about the most basic thing i was building on and honestly everything after it got simpler. still ripping out the old assumptions though

#buildinpublic #aiagents #multiagent #devtools #mcp #agentops #founder #aiengineering

title: The 7-field handoff that replaced my transcript dumps
hook: 7 fields. zero transcripts. that's my whole handoff.
hypothesis: a numbered framework hook + one dense screenshot-able list slide drives saves and shares harder than a personal narrative arc does
caption:
i watched two of my agents 'collaborate' by one of them pasting a 300-message transcript to the other and it was so obviously broken. like the second agent had to reverse-engineer the goal, the decisions, what was already tried, all of it, from a wall of text. so i started writing down what a handoff actually needs to carry and it turned into 7 fields: goal, definition of done, decisions + why, permissions, budget, confidence, next action. that's the pack. structured context instead of 'here's everything we said, you figure out what mattered.' and the part that got me is once the handoff carries the why + the bar, work below the threshold just loops back before it ever burns my review time. the transcript was never the artifact. the compiled context is

title: Your agents don't have a memory problem
hook: your agents don't have a memory problem.
hypothesis: a single contrarian reframe (memory vs continuity) + a comment-bait CTA beats a build-log narrative for cold-reach engagement and shares
caption:
someone in my dms was like 'i just need my agents to remember more' and i sat with that for a second, because i used to think the exact same thing. and so we all keep reaching for the same fix — bigger context window, better retrieval, tighter summaries — and the agent still shows up to the next task not knowing what we already decided or what 'done' even means here. right? and that's when it hit me that remembering the conversation and remembering the work are two completely different problems. memory is 'what did we say.' continuity is 'why does this exist + what's the bar + who approves.' the chat can't hold that, because the chat ends. so orgx keeps it in a work graph underneath the client — decisions, approvals, receipts, the quality bar — and the agents read from that instead of from a transcript. anyway i keep watching people optimize the memory and skip the continuity entirely

#aiagents #buildinpublic #multiagent #agentops #mcp #llm #devtools

title: You're handing off a transcript. That's the bug.
hook: the transcript is not the handoff.
hypothesis: A mistake-callout hook ('that's the bug') plus a numbered 7-field anatomy list (save-bait) drives saves + shares harder than a pure thesis hook for cold reach.
caption:
watched a friend hand a half-finished feature off from claude to cursor last week by literally copy-pasting the entire thread. like 60k tokens of back-and-forth. and cursor spent its first ten minutes re-deriving what they'd already settled, then quietly picked a different auth approach because the *why* never crossed over. and i'm like, that's the bug, right there. a transcript is a record of how the work happened, but the next agent doesn't need how. it needs the goal + the definition of done + the decisions and why you landed on them + what it's even allowed to touch. that's a context pack, not a chat log. the prompt ends but the work keeps moving, and if all you pass forward is the transcript, the org forgets why the work exists the second it changes hands...

#aiagents #promptengineering #claude #cursor #buildinpublic #aiops #mcp #devtools

title: 5 doors your context dies at
hook: your context dies at 5 specific doors.
hypothesis: a numbered 'X doors it dies at' save-bait list (screenshot-first, 8 slides) drives higher saves/shares than a single emotional scene, even at the cost of a slightly slower first-slide read
caption:
i counted it once — in a single afternoon i re-explained the same feature goal five separate times. once handing from Claude to Codex, once when i moved repos, once switching to Cursor for the frontend, once to a teammate, and once to myself on friday when i'd already forgotten why i started. and none of those were 'losing' context in some vague way, they were five specific doors and the context died at every single one. that's when it clicked that context isn't a transcript you scroll back through hoping the answer's buried in there, it's a graph the org is supposed to keep — the decisions, the approvals, the artifacts, the receipts, living underneath the client instead of trapped inside one conversation. because the task outlives the chat, always, the chat is the most disposable part of the whole thing and somehow we made it the primitive. so i'm building the layer that sits beneath Claude and Cursor and Codex and just remembers — the goal, the bar, the why — so every door is a pass-through instead of a reset. anyway. five times in one afternoon, that number still

title: Approving every agent action is why your fleet doesn't scale.
hook: approving every agent action is the reason you can't run a fleet.
hypothesis: A contrarian bold-claim hook ('approving everything is why you can't scale') plus a named-boundary list out-performs a soft educational hook for saves + comment volume.
caption:
i counted the approval prompts my agents threw at me one afternoon and it was somewhere north of 40. forty times i clicked 'yes go ahead' on stuff like 'can i read this file' and 'can i write this draft.' and by like the fifth one i'm rubber-stamping without reading, which means the one approval that actually mattered — an agent about to send an email to a client — got the exact same reflexive yes as reading a file. that's the failure. human review should scale with consequence, not activity. so the escalation model in orgx just flips it: reversible stuff runs, and the gate only closes on the handful of things you can't take back. publishing, payments, outbound messages, merges. and anything high-risk it's never seen fails closed instead of guessing. it's not fewer guardrails, it's guardrails that are actually where the danger is...

title: You're approving the wrong things
hook: reversible. ambiguous. irreversible. only one should reach you.
hypothesis: a 'you're doing X wrong' mistake-callout hook plus a single reframe line ('scale review with consequence, not activity') beats a framework list for cold reach
caption:
hit a point a few weeks ago where I was drowning in approve/deny prompts from my own agents and realized I'd basically rebuilt the exact job I was trying to get rid of. like every single step wanted a thumbs up. and most of them did not matter at all, renaming a file, drafting a doc, whatever. but buried in there was the one that could actually message a client or merge into main. so it clicked, I don't need to review activity, I need to review consequence. reversible + cheap, let it run. irreversible or ambiguous, that's mine, and everything else is just policy: publishing, payments, outbound messages, merges gate at the human boundary and an unknown high-risk tool fails closed instead of guessing. autonomy is useful but it's worthless if I'm still the bottleneck on every keystroke. still tuning exactly where the line sits but

title: The 7-step loop your agents keep breaking
hook: real work runs one 7-step loop. agents break it.
hypothesis: a numbered save-bait framework (the 7-step loop) drives saves + follows better than a pure teardown for the mental-models pillar
caption:
watched an agent nail a task last week and then completely lose the thread the second I handed it to the next one. and I'm sitting there like, it didn't forget the WORK. it forgot why the work existed. goal + definition of done + the one decision that made the whole thing make sense, gone. so I started drawing it out and it's always the same shape: goal → plan → work → decision → artifact → proof → next action. seven steps, and every agent setup I've seen runs like four of them and calls it done. the transcript remembers what happened, nothing remembers why, and that's the whole bet with OrgX honestly, the conversation was never supposed to hold continuity, the org is. close that last arrow and every rep starts where the last one ended instead of from zero. anyway I keep finding new places the loop breaks

title: your agents don't have a memory problem, your org does
hook: your agents remember fine. your org forgets.
hypothesis: a reframe-diagnosis hook ('not a memory problem, an org problem') anchored by a 7-field handoff framework slide maximizes screenshot-saves vs a single-number payoff
caption:
someone told me their agents have a memory problem and i pushed back kind of hard, maybe too hard. because it's not the agents. the agents are fine. the problem is you handed off with a three-line summary and expected the next one to inherit an entire company's worth of context from it. a summary tells you what happened. it doesn't carry why it matters — the quality bar, the decision you already made and killed, the budget, the thing you're NOT allowed to do. so the next agent re-derives all of it from scratch and of course it drifts. that's not a memory problem, that's an org that never wrote down how it thinks. so we compile the handoff — goal + definition of done + decisions and why + permissions + budget + confidence + next action — and anything under the bar loops back before it ever hits your desk. the next agent needs more than a summary. it needs the org to actually remember

title: the prompt was the wrong primitive
hook: we built everything on the wrong primitive.
hypothesis: a thesis-declaration hook ('the prompt was the wrong primitive') + a quotable close beats a problem-first teardown for cold reach on a skeptical AI-infra audience
caption:
i wrote the cleanest prompt of my life last tuesday. genuinely proud of it. the agent shipped exactly what i wanted and then i closed the tab and it was just... gone. and so i'm sitting there like wait — the thing that knew the goal + the tradeoffs + why we picked postgres over the thing we almost picked, that all lived in a conversation i just deleted. that's when it clicked that the prompt was never the primitive. the conversation can't be the thing that remembers your company, right? the org has to. so orgx passes a compiled handoff instead of a transcript — goal, definition of done, decisions and why, budget, next action — and the work lives in a graph, not a thread that dies when you hit close. the prompt ends. what keeps moving after is the whole point and almost nobody's building for that part yet

title: you approve every agent action — that's not oversight
hook: you're the slowest agent in your fleet.
hypothesis: a mistake-callout hook ('you approve every action — that's noise') + a save-bait tool-policy list drives more saves and comments than a pure thesis carousel
caption:
watched a founder friend demo his agent setup last month, he had like 30 agents running and he was so proud, and then i noticed he was clicking approve every four seconds. just approve approve approve. so i asked him when's the last time you actually said no, and he went quiet. right? because that's the tell — if you approve everything you're not reviewing anything, you're just a very slow queue with a pulse. and most of what agents do is reversible anyway. drafting, planning, iterating, who cares, let it run. the moment that actually needs you is the irreversible one: the publish, the payment, the merge, the message that can't be unsent. so gate THAT. tool policy sits at the boundary, unknown high-risk tool fails closed, everything else just moves. escalate consequence, not activity. your attention is the scarcest thing in the whole loop and you're burning it on keystrokes

#aiagents #aiops #agentic #humanintheloop #aiinfra #buildinpublic #multiagent

title: 'Done' is not proof
hook: your agent said 'done.' that's a vibe, not proof.
hypothesis: a provocation hook that reframes a word everyone uses ('done' is a vibe) plus a screenshot-able 'what a receipt carries' list tests whether challenge-style hooks outperform mistake-callouts
caption:
someone asked me last week how I actually trust the work my agents ship and I gave this long answer and then realized the honest version is way simpler: I don't trust 'done.' 'done' is a vibe. an agent typing a checkmark at the end of a transcript tells me nothing about whether the thing is right. and the two options everyone defaults to are both bad, either I re-check all of it myself which means I didn't really delegate, or I trust it blind which is how you wake up to something ugly in prod. so the reframe that actually fixed it: the artifact is the receipt. work comes back with its version + provenance + how it was evaluated + what review state it's in, proof I can read in ten seconds without re-running anything. and the stuff under the quality bar loops back before it ever reaches my attention, and it shows up right inside Claude or Cursor so I'm not leaving to go verify. still think most agent tools are shipping vibes not receipts but

title: you didn't lose the code, you lost the why
hook: the code survived the handoff. the why didn't.
hypothesis: a 'you didn't lose X, you lost Y' reframe hook + a screenshot-worthy context-pack field list beats a straight product explainer for cold saves
caption:
watched a friend hand a half-built feature from Claude to Codex last week and the second agent just confidently rebuilt the thing they'd already decided NOT to build. and he's scrolling back through the chat like where did i say that, and the answer is he didn't, it was never in the chat, it was in his head. that's the part nobody talks about — the transcript keeps every keystroke and none of the why. so you paste 10k tokens of conversation into the next agent and it's technically 'context' but it can't act on any of it, doesn't know the definition of done or the three things you already ruled out or how much budget is left. and so i keep landing on the same thing: the prompt was the wrong primitive. the conversation can't hold the goal across a boundary, the org has to — a compiled handoff, goal + decisions + why + permissions + next action, passed as structure instead of a chat dump. and once you see it you can't unsee it, every handoff you've ever done was really just

title: 'Done' is not proof. Here's what a receipt actually contains.
hook: 'done' is a claim. a receipt is proof.
hypothesis: A word-kill callout hook ('done is not proof') plus a 5-field receipt-anatomy list tests whether reframing a familiar word out-reaches a problem-first hook for cold traffic + saves.
caption:
the thing that finally broke me on agent workflows was realizing i didn't trust a single 'done' i got back. an agent would come back all confident, task complete, and i'd still open every file and re-read every diff, because 'done' just means the agent stopped — it says nothing about whether the work is right. and so i'm re-auditing everything by hand, which means the autonomy never compounds, i'm just a slower reviewer with extra steps. so the fix isn't a better status message. the artifact has to come back as the receipt: version, provenance, how it was evaluated, what review state it's in, what it cost, all bolted to the thing itself. and then proof rooms + embedded mcp widgets render that state right inside claude or cursor so you're never leaving to go verify. the whole idea is you read the receipt instead of redoing the work...

#aiagents #mcp #buildinpublic #aiops #claude #agentic #devtools #trustbutverify

title: activity up, confidence down
hook: your agents got busier. you got less sure.
hypothesis: an inverse-correlation paradox hook (activity up, confidence down) + a danger→teal color arc outperforms a positive product-benefit hook for cold reach with the skeptic audience
caption:
the moment that made me start OrgX: i had six agents running, the dashboard was all green, and i felt worse than when i was doing everything by hand. activity went straight up and my confidence went straight down, and those two aren't supposed to move opposite directions but they do the second you're orchestrating instead of typing. and i figured out why — every unit of work was asking for the same slice of my attention. a typo fix and a payment endpoint both showing up as 'review me', same size, same weight. so you either rubber-stamp the batch and something irreversible slips through, or you re-read all of it and you're the bottleneck again, congrats you built an expensive way to do your own job. the fix was never more review. it's escalating consequence, not activity — reserve the human boundary for the stuff that can't be undone, publish, payments, merges, and let everything under the bar loop back before it hits your desk. that's the whole difference between autonomy that quietly stresses you out and autonomy that actually
